Solving linear systems with matrices

A system of linear equations can be written compactly as Ax=b, where A holds the coefficients, x the unknowns and b the right-hand sides. This form is how engineers solve circuit equations, truss forces and many other problems. Choose one of three matrix methods and enter the augmented matrix [A∣b]; every step is shown with exact fractions.

Try changing the input

Solve the same system with all three methods: the answer is identical, but the work involved differs a lot — especially as the system grows.

Methods

Gauss–Jordan elimination
Row-reduce [A∣b] to [I∣x]. Works for every system and detects inconsistent (no solution) and dependent (infinitely many) systems.
Cramer's rule
xj=det⁡Ajdet⁡A, where Aj is A with column j replaced by b. Requires det⁡A≠0.
Inverse matrix
x=A−1b. Also requires det⁡A≠0; useful when the same A is used with many right-hand sides.

Worked example

Cramer's rule for 3x+2y=16, 4x−y=3

Step 1 — Determinant of A

det⁡A=∣324−1∣=−3−8=−11

Step 2 — Replace columns by b

det⁡Ax=∣1623−1∣=−22,det⁡Ay=∣31643∣=−55

Step 3 — Divide

x=−22−11=2,y=−55−11=5

Input format and limits

  • One equation per line: the coefficients followed by the right-hand side. A | before the last number is optional.
  • Square systems from 2×2 up to 6×6. If det⁡A=0, Cramer's rule and the inverse method cannot be used; the calculator says so and uses elimination to classify the system.
  • All arithmetic is exact.
